In the context of rule mining, which is our particular focus, these goals translate into generating an abstract (summarized) KG on which inference rules can be mined much faster than on the original KG, while providing losslessness of the mined rules. We define losslessness for rule mining as the rule-mining process being able to obtain from the abstract KG generated by GAME+ all of the inference rules that can be mined from the original input KG. The flow of the proposed GAME+ approach is outlined in Fig. 1 . Intuitively, GAME+ first clusters nodes based on a given similarity-scoring function for KG nodes and then fuses the nodes in each cluster together, along with their incident edges, such that the KG data sizes are reduced by elimination of repetitive triples. Together, the two stages of KG summarization in the GAME+ approach aim to address the challenges of scaling rule mining to big graph data in the presence of data irregularity, while delivering on the lossless preservation of the rules that can be mined from the summarized GAME+ output. In fact, our experimental results reported in this paper suggest that our proposed KG-abstraction approach can substantially reduce the sizes of the original KGs, leading to much faster performance of rule mining on the resulting abstract KGs, while also enabling mining on the abstract KGs of all of the inference rules that can be obtained from the original KGs. Our specific contributions are as follows 3 We formalize the problem of lossless KG abstraction (summarization) for downstream analytics, with a particular focus on rule mining; We introduce a domain- and application-independent approach called GAME+, which generates a reduced KG that is lossless for rule mining while improving the rule-mining efficiency; We prove that our KG abstraction approach is lossless by introducing an inverse approach that can recover the original KG in its entirety from the abstract KG; We present the results of a case study performed by a biomedical expert, which suggest that the node-clustering phase of the proposed approach can cluster nodes that are meaningfully related and that the resulting clusters can be insightful to biomedical experts; and We report experimental results on three large-scale, real-world biomedical KGs (DRKG [ 24 ], Hetionet [ 25 ], and ROBOKOP [ 9 ]); the results indicate that the proposed approach is promising for generating reduced KGs that are lossless for efficient rule mining; additionally, the results of performing data reductions at various summarization levels highlight potential trade-offs between the improvements in mining efficiency and the effectiveness of the rule-mining outcomes. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we review related work. In Section 3 we provide the necessary background information and the problem statement for our work. In Section 4 we introduce the proposed GAME+ approach, and in Section 5 we present and discuss our experimental results, followed by our case-study results in Section 6 . We conclude in Section 7 . Related work Our work in this paper is closely related to knowledge-graph (KG) summarization work [ 10 , 11 – 12 ], which has received much attention in recent years. KG-summarization approaches have been developed for purposes including graph visualization [ 15 ], graph cleaning [ 16 ], recommender systems [ 17 ], efficient query evaluation [ 18 ], other graph exploration [ 19 , 20 – 21 ], and KG-size reduction [ 20 , 22 ]. There have also been efforts toward generating domain-specific graph summaries [ 19 ] and personalized graph summaries for users [ 23 ]. Unfortunately, many KG-summarization approaches may result in loss of valuable information for KG analytics such as rule mining. In contrast, our proposed approach can enable effective KG rule mining due to its losslessness property. The KG-summarization approaches most similar to ours are those of [ 15 , 16 ]. The approach of [ 15 ] introduces the concepts of abstract nodes and abstract edges, which are similar to the concepts of consolidated nodes and consolidated edges that we introduce in Section 3.2 . (We opt for the term “consolidated,” as it better captures the purpose of these nodes and edges in our proposed approach.) In addition, the approach of [ 15 ] uses the same node-similarity function as the one considered in this paper, see Section 5.1.3 . At the same time, the summarization approach of [ 15 ] applies to KGs whose edge labels are all the same, unlike our approach, which is applicable to KGs that can have any number of different edge labels. In addition, the approach of [ 15 ] uses the common k-means algorithm for node clustering, whereas we introduce our own node-clustering algorithm. Two key challenges arise when using k-means for KG summarization: It relies both on predefined numbers of clusters and predefined seed nodes. As appropriate values for these parameters are difficult to determine in many scenarios, our proposed node-clustering approach does not rely on such parameters, see Section 4.2 . Moreover, the approach of [ 15 ] specifically targets improving KG visualization, whereas we aim to reduce the size of the KG for downstream analytical tasks, such as rule mining. The approach of [ 16 ] also generates abstract KGs; however, the goal of their work is to perform graph cleaning, specifically, consistency checking, which is accomplished via their abstract KGs. Because the approach of [ 16 ] focuses on resolving ontological inconsistencies in the data, their abstract KGs rise entirely to the ontological level and do not preserve instance information. While such an abstraction is sufficient for consistency checking, it is insufficient for many other downstream analysis tasks, such as the task of rule mining, which is our focus in this paper.
